Beef and Broccoli

4.8
(9)
8 Reviews

An umami-rich sauce and a simple technique for tender beef are the keys to this American Chinese classic.

By
Breana Lai Killeen
Breana Lai Killeen
Breana Lai Killeen, M.P.H., RD, is a food editor, recipe developer, farmer and dietitian who has worked in all facets of the food world. She has more than 20 years of experience cooking professionally, pouring wine, and creating editorial and digital content for top brands.
Food & Wine's Editorial Guidelines
Updated on September 13, 2026
Total Time:
30 mins
Servings:
4
  • Velveting the beef with baking soda and cornstarch ensures it stays tender and silky, just like in restaurant stir-fries.
  • The oyster sauce–soy sauce blend delivers deep umami flavor, balanced by crisp-tender broccoli for freshness and crunch.
  • This dish comes together in half an hour, making it ideal for a flavorful weeknight dinner.

Beef and broccoli is a cornerstone of American Chinese cooking, beloved for its balance of protein, vegetables, and an umami-packed sauce. This recipe captures the essence of the dish with a focus on achieving that restaurant-style texture and flavor. The secret lies in a technique called velveting, which uses baking soda and cornstarch to tenderize the beef, ensuring it cooks up juicy and silky. This step, combined with high-heat cooking, keeps the meat from drying out while delivering that classic takeout feel.

The sauce here is another star. A blend of oyster sauce, soy sauce, Shaoxing wine (or dry sherry), sugar, and aromatics like ginger and garlic, it clings beautifully to the beef and broccoli without being overly saucy, making it ideal to spoon over steamed rice. Broccoli florets are quickly steamed until crisp-tender, providing freshness and crunch to balance the richness of the beef.

Best of all, this dish comes together in 30 minutes. It’s perfect for a weeknight dinner but impressive enough to serve for friends. Once you’ve mastered velveting, you can use the technique with other proteins, like chicken or shrimp, expanding your stir-fry repertoire.

What is velveting?

Velveting is a classic Chinese cooking technique that involves marinating thinly sliced protein, often beef, chicken, or shrimp, in a mixture that may include baking soda, cornstarch, egg white, soy sauce, or rice wine. The baking soda slightly raises the meat’s pH, helping it retain moisture, while cornstarch forms a protective coating. 

After marinating, the meat is briefly stir-fried in a hot pan, resulting in a velvety texture. Beyond beef and broccoli, velveting is commonly used in dishes like chicken with cashews, shrimp stir-fries, and other Chinese American classics. 

Notes from the Food & Wine Test Kitchen

  • If the steak is difficult to slice, freeze it for 15 minutes uncovered on a plate. Freezing the meat will make it firmer and easier to cut.
  • Slice beef thinly against the grain for the best texture.
  • Don’t overcrowd the pan when cooking beef. It’s better to cook it in two batches for proper browning.

Suggested pairing 

Pair the beef and broccoli with a crisp, aromatic white wine like a dry Riesling or Gewürztraminer. The wine’s natural sweetness balances the savory, umami-rich sauce and highlights the ginger and garlic notes. If you prefer beer, a light lager or pilsner provides a refreshing contrast to the dish’s richness. For a nonalcoholic option, jasmine tea or sparkling water with citrus pairs well, too.

This recipe was developed by Julia Levy; the text was written by Breana Killeen.

Keep Screen Awake

Ingredients

Oops! Something went wrong. Our team is working on it.

This recipe was developed at its original yield. Ingredient amounts are automatically adjusted, but cooking times and steps remain unchanged. Note that not all recipes scale perfectly. Original recipe (1X) yields 4 servings

  • 1 teaspoon baking soda

  • 1/3 cup, plus 2 tablespoons water, divided

  • 4 tablespoons vegetable oil, divided

  • 2 tablespoons oyster sauce, divided

  • 2 tablespoons Shaoxing wine or dry sherry, divided

  • 1 tablespoon, plus 2 teaspoons soy sauce, divided

  • 1 tablespoon, plus 1 teaspoon cornstarch, divided

  • 2 teaspoons granulated sugar, divided

  • 12 ounces flank steak, cut into 1/2-inch strips

  • 12 ounces fresh broccoli, cut into 1 1/2-inch florets (about 4 cups)

  • 1 bunch scallions, trimmed and cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces (about 1 1/4 cups)

  • 1 (1/2-inch) piece fresh ginger, peeled and thinly sliced (about 1 tablespoon)

  • 3 garlic cloves, minced (about 1 tablespoon)

  • 1 tablespoon toasted sesame oil

  • Toasted sesame seeds

  • Steamed white rice

Directions

  1. Whisk together baking soda, 2 tablespoons water, 1 tablespoon oil, 1 tablespoon oyster sauce, 1 tablespoon Shaoxing wine, 1 tablespoon soy sauce, 1 tablespoon cornstarch, and 1 teaspoon sugar in a medium bowl. Add steak strips, and toss to coat. Set aside at room temperature, stirring occasionally, for 10 minutes.

  2. Meanwhile, whisk together remaining 1 tablespoon oyster sauce, 1 tablespoon Shaoxing wine, 2 teaspoons soy sauce, 1 teaspoon cornstarch, and 1 teaspoon sugar in a medium bowl. Set aside.

  3. Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a wok or large cast iron skillet over high until just smoking. Add broccoli; cook, stirring constantly, until starting to turn bright green, about 30 seconds. Add remaining 1/3 cup water; cover and reduce heat to medium. Steam broccoli until tender-crisp, about 3 minutes; transfer to a paper towel-lined plate.

  4. Return wok or skillet to high heat, allowing any excess water to evaporate, if necessary. Once dry, add remaining 2 tablespoons oil to wok, and swirl to coat; reduce heat to medium-high. Using tongs or a slotted spoon, add half of steak strips from marinade to wok, allowing excess marinade to drip off; cook, undisturbed, until starting to turn brown, about 1 minute. Flip steak strips, and cook until mostly browned, about 1 minute more. Push browned steak strips to the side of wok, and repeat cooking process with remaining strips. (Discard remaining marinade.) Push all steak strips to the sides of wok. Add scallions, ginger, and garlic to empty part of wok; cook, stirring constantly, until fragrant, 15 to 20 seconds. Stir steak strips into mixture; return broccoli to wok, and toss to combine. Whisk oyster sauce mixture until combined; add to wok, and cook, stirring constantly, until sauce is thickened and evenly distributed, about 30 seconds. Transfer beef and broccoli to a platter, and drizzle with sesame oil. Sprinkle with sesame seeds, and serve with rice.

Make ahead


Broccoli can be trimmed and steamed up to 3 days ahead. Leftovers keep well in the fridge for up to 3 days. Don’t marinate (aka velvet) the beef for more than 1 hour; any longer and it may turn mealy.
